caption:
Why was the SS Great Eastern a failure?

She was 692 feet long, launched in 1858, and designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel to carry 4,000 people to Australia without refuelling. No longer ship was built until 1899. No heavier one until 1901. Nobody matched her passenger capacity until 1913.

The first launch attempt, in November 1857, failed: she stuck on her rails and two men were killed. Renting out chains and jacks for the second attempt made engineer Richard Tangye's fortune — "We launched Great Eastern, and she launched us."

As a liner she lost money on almost every crossing. In 1862 she struck an uncharted rock off Montauk Point that opened a gash 83 feet long in her outer hull; her double skin held, but no drydock in the world was big enough to repair her. Her one real success was cable: in 1866 she landed the first lasting transatlantic telegraph cable at Heart's Content, Newfoundland.

She finished as a showboat and a floating advertisement for Lewis's department store on the Mersey, and was broken up from 1889 — 18 months of work, the double hull the hardest part.

Still unresolved: the story that shipbreakers found a worker sealed inside her double hull. It spread after her scrapping and fills nautical ghost-story books, but authors including L. T. C. Rolt dismissed it, noting such a find would have been logged and reported. An anchor recovered in 2007 near Great Eastern Rock may or may not be hers.

Images: Robert Howlett's 1857 shipyard photographs, a deck plan by W. H. Webb, the Lewis's advertising view at Liverpool from Royal Museums Greenwich, and Allan C. Green's photograph of her beached for breaking. All public domain.

cards.note: He collapsed from a stroke after being photographed on her deck. He died ten days later, four days after her first sea trials.

cards.alt: Man in top hat, cigar in mouth, standing before giant iron chain links.

cards.headline: <y>The first launch failed.</y> She stuck on the rails.
cards.note: 3 November 1857: two men killed, the ship stranded. At 19,000 tons she was the heaviest object humans had moved.
cards.alt: Workers beside enormous chain drums at a shipyard, ship hull behind them.

cards.headline: An uncharted rock cut a gash <y>83 feet long</y> in her hull.
cards.note: 1862, off Montauk Point. Her double skin held — and no drydock in the world was big enough to repair her.

cards.headline: The ship that laid the Atlantic cable became an <y>advertising hoarding</y>.
cards.note: In 1866 she landed the first lasting transatlantic telegraph cable. By 1886 she was selling Lewis's department store on the Mersey.
cards.alt: Long six-masted ship, hull painted with LEWIS'S store slogans, at anchor.

cards.headline: Scrapped in 1889 — <y>still the largest ship</y> ever built.
cards.note: Breaking her up took 18 months. Rumours of a worker sealed in her double hull have been dismissed, but never fully settled.
